title: FileOutputStream — write bytes to a file
description: Write the string 'Hello, Java IO!' to a file called 'hello.txt' using FileOutputStream.
starterCode:
// Write "Hello, Java IO!" to hello.txt using FileOutputStream
// Use getBytes() to convert String to byte[]

solution.explanation: FileOutputStream writes raw bytes to a file. getBytes() converts the String to a byte[] using the platform's default charset (use getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8) for explicit encoding). The try-with-resources statement (Java 7+) automatically closes the stream even if an exception occurs — always use this pattern with IO resources. The file is created if it doesn't exist; it is truncated if it does (use FileOutputStream(file, true) to append).

solution.explanation: FileInputStream reads raw bytes from a file. read(byte[]) fills the buffer and returns the number of bytes actually read (-1 at end of file). Creating a String from a byte array: new String(bytes, offset, length) — always specify offset 0 and the actual bytesRead to avoid including leftover zeros in the buffer. For large files, use a loop checking bytesRead != -1. For modern code, prefer Files.readAllBytes() or Files.readString().

title: BufferedInputStream/OutputStream — efficient byte copy
description: Copy a file efficiently using BufferedInputStream and BufferedOutputStream. Buffering reduces system calls by reading/writing in large chunks.
starterCode:
// Create source file with some content
// Copy source.txt to destination.txt using buffered byte streams

solution.explanation: Wrapping a FileInputStream in a BufferedInputStream adds an in-memory buffer (default 8192 bytes). Each read() call fills the buffer from disk if needed, then serves subsequent reads from memory — dramatically reducing OS-level disk reads. The same applies to BufferedOutputStream which batches small writes into large disk writes. The Decorator pattern: Buffered wraps FileInput/Output without changing the API. Always close in reverse order of opening — try-with-resources handles this automatically.

title: DataInputStream/DataOutputStream — primitive types
description: Write an int, a double, and a boolean to a binary file using DataOutputStream. Read them back in the same order with DataInputStream.
starterCode:
// Write: int 42, double 3.14, boolean true
// Read them back and verify

solution.explanation: DataOutputStream writes Java primitives as fixed-size binary data: int=4 bytes, double=8 bytes, boolean=1 byte. DataInputStream reads them back. The critical rule: you MUST read in exactly the same order and types as written — there are no field names in the binary format. writeUTF/readUTF uses a modified UTF-8 encoding with a 2-byte length prefix. This is different from Java object serialization — it's manual but efficient.

title: ObjectOutputStream — serialize a Java object
description: Serialize a User object (name + age) to a file using ObjectOutputStream. The class must implement Serializable.
starterCode:
// Define a Serializable User class with name and age
// Serialize a User to user.ser using ObjectOutputStream

solution.explanation: Java serialization converts an object's state to a byte stream. The class must implement Serializable (a marker interface). serialVersionUID is a version identifier — always declare it explicitly to prevent InvalidClassException when the class changes. Fields marked transient are excluded from serialization. Wrap in BufferedOutputStream for efficiency. Modern alternatives: Jackson JSON, Protocol Buffers, or Java records with custom converters.

title: FileWriter and FileReader — character streams
description: Write multiple lines of text to a file using FileWriter, then read them back using FileReader.
starterCode:
// Write 3 lines to notes.txt using FileWriter
// Read them back using FileReader

solution.explanation: FileWriter and FileReader are character streams — they work with char, not byte. They use the platform default charset for encoding/decoding. For explicit charset: new FileWriter(file, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) (Java 11+). Character streams inherit from Writer/Reader, not OutputStream/InputStream. Use these for text files where you care about character encoding; use byte streams for binary data.

title: BufferedReader — read file line by line
description: Use BufferedReader to read a text file line by line and number each line in the output.
hints: Use a loop: String line; while ((line = br.readLine()) != null)

solution.explanation: BufferedReader adds buffering to a Reader, dramatically improving performance. readLine() reads one line at a time (strips the line terminator) and returns null at end-of-file. The while ((line = br.readLine()) != null) idiom is the canonical Java way to read a text file line by line. Modern alternative: Files.lines(path) returns a Stream<String> for functional processing. BufferedReader also has a lines() method returning Stream<String> (Java 8+).

title: BufferedWriter and PrintWriter
description: Write structured data to a file using BufferedWriter. Then do the same with PrintWriter's convenient println. Understand the difference between the two.
starterCode:
// Write 3 lines using BufferedWriter (manual newLine())
// Write 3 lines using PrintWriter (auto println)

solution.explanation: BufferedWriter wraps a Writer for efficiency. newLine() writes the OS-specific line separator (\r\n on Windows, \n on Unix). PrintWriter builds on top — it adds println(), print(), printf() and crucially does NOT declare checked exceptions (errors are silent unless you check checkError()). Always wrap FileWriter in BufferedWriter before PrintWriter for efficiency. PrintWriter(String filename) is a shortcut that wraps it all.

title: Write a CSV file
description: Write a list of Product objects (id, name, price) to a CSV file using PrintWriter.
hints: Then one line per product with comma separator

solution.explanation: CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is just plain text with commas as delimiters. Key points: (1) always include a header row for readability, (2) use printf for formatted numeric output, (3) if values can contain commas or newlines, wrap in quotes: '"' + value + '"'. For production use OpenCSV or Apache Commons CSV which handle quoting, escaping, and edge cases. PrintWriter.printf with %n is portable (uses OS line separator).

methodSignatures.description: Formats and writes text. Use %s for strings, %d for int, %.2f for double, %n for newline.

title: Read and parse a CSV file
description: Read the products.csv file line by line, skip the header, split each line by comma, and reconstruct Product objects.

solution.explanation: Parsing CSV: split() on comma gives an array of fields. trim() removes whitespace. Parse numeric fields with Integer.parseInt()/Double.parseDouble(). Always skip the header with a single readLine() before the main loop. Edge cases: fields with commas need quoting (then don't use simple split). The .trim() is defensive coding for files with spaces after commas. Using streams: br.lines().skip(1).map(line -> ...).collect(toList()) is the modern approach.

title: CSV with Scanner
description: Use Scanner to read a CSV file, using comma as the delimiter. Count how many products have price > 50.

solution.explanation: Scanner is a versatile token-based parser. useDelimiter() sets a regex used to split input — here `,|\r?\n` matches comma or newline (handles Windows/Unix). nextInt(), next(), nextDouble() consume the next token as the respective type. hasNextInt() checks if the next token is an integer — stops cleanly when there are no more full rows. Scanner is convenient for simple CSVs but slower than BufferedReader for large files.

title: Write a Java object to JSON using Jackson
description: Serialize a Product object to a JSON file using Jackson's ObjectMapper.

solution.explanation: Jackson's ObjectMapper is the central serialization/deserialization engine. writeValue(File, Object) serializes the object to a file. writeValueAsString(Object) returns the JSON as a String. INDENT_OUTPUT enables pretty-printing (2-space indentation). By default Jackson uses public fields or public getters. For private fields add @JsonProperty or configure the mapper. ObjectMapper is thread-safe and expensive to create — typically a singleton.

title: Read JSON into a Java object (deserialization)
description: Deserialize the product.json file back into a Product object using Jackson's readValue.
starterCode:
// Read product.json and deserialize to Product object
// Access fields and print

solution.explanation: readValue(source, Class<T>) deserializes JSON into an instance of the given class. Jackson requires a no-arg constructor for deserialization (or @JsonCreator on a constructor). The source can be a File, String, InputStream, URL, byte[], or Reader. If the JSON has extra fields not in the class, Jackson throws UnrecognizedPropertyException by default — configure FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES to false: mapper.configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false).

title: Read a JSON array into a List
description: Deserialize a JSON array of products into a List<Product> using TypeReference.

solution.explanation: For generic types like List<Product>, you can't pass List.class because of Java type erasure — the generic type info is lost at runtime. TypeReference<T> is Jackson's solution: it captures the generic type at compile time using an anonymous subclass pattern (the {} after the constructor). The new TypeReference<List<Product>>() {} creates an anonymous subclass whose type parameters are preserved and accessible via reflection.

methodSignatures.description: Captures generic type information at compile time. Use as: new TypeReference<List<Product>>() {}

title: JSON to Map and tree navigation
description: Deserialize a JSON object to Map<String, Object> (schema-free). Also use JsonNode for tree navigation without POJO classes.

solution.explanation: Map<String,Object> deserialization is schema-free: JSON objects become LinkedHashMaps, arrays become ArrayLists, numbers become Integer/Long/Double. JsonNode provides a DOM-like tree API. get(fieldName) navigates object fields; asInt()/asDouble()/asText() extract typed values. For arrays: iterate with for-each or get(index). Use path() instead of get() for safe navigation — path() returns MissingNode instead of null for non-existent fields.
